It was also said: knowledge and understanding. "And I do not wish to oppose you by doing what I forbid you from. I wish only reform as far as I am able. My success is only through Allah; upon Him I rely, and to Him I turn back," that is, I return to Him in whatever calamities befall me. It was also said: to Him I return in the Hereafter.

"And O my people, let not my dissension (shiqaq) cause you [to commit] — let not my opposition and separation induce you — that there befall you the like of what befell the people of Nuh, or the people of Hud, or the people of Salih," of punishment; "and the people of Lut are not far from you." That is because they were recent in time to the destruction of the people of Lut. It was also said: the dwelling of the people of Lut is not far from you. "And O my people, seek forgiveness of your Lord, then turn to Him in repentance. Indeed my Lord is Merciful, Loving (wadud)," loving the believers. It was also said: beloved to the believers and loved by them.

They said: "O Shu'ayb, we do not understand much of what you say, and indeed we see you among us as weak." That was because he was blind. Sufyan said: "He was weak of sight," and it was said of him: "the orator of the prophets." "And were it not for your clan," your tribe, and he had might and protection from his people, "we would have stoned you," we would have killed you. "And you are not mighty against us."

He said: "O my people, is my clan more esteemed by you than Allah, and you have cast Him behind your backs?" It was said: the pronoun refers to Allah; and it was said: to the command of Allah and what Shu'ayb brought, meaning you have thrown it behind your backs and abandoned it. It is said: "I placed my affair behind my back" when one neglects his affair and fails in his duty.

"Indeed my Lord is encompassing of what you do. And O my people, act according to your position (makanah)," that is, your deliberation and station. It is said: "So-and-so acts according to his status (makanah) and standing (makanah)" when he acts with deliberation and settles. And it is said: "makana, yamkunu, makanan, makanah." "Indeed I am acting; you will know" which of us is the one who brings harm upon himself and is more misguided in his action. That is His saying: "Who will receive a punishment that disgraces him, and who is a liar." It was said: ("man") is in the accusative position, meaning "you will know who is the liar." It was also said: "and He will disgrace the one who is a liar." It was also said: its position is nominative, its estimation being: "and who is a liar, so his lie will be known, and he will taste the consequence of his affair." "So wait," and expect the punishment. "Indeed I am with you as a watcher, expecting."

When Our command came, We saved Shu'ayb and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us, and the Cry seized those who did wrong: a cry from the sky seized them and destroyed them. It is said: Jibril cried out at them with one cry, and their souls left their bodies.

So they were found in their homes, prostrate, dead, fallen, slain, as if they had never dwelt there. "Away with them!" Destruction and wrath, "as Madyan was made distant" when Thamud perished.

And We certainly sent Musa with Our signs and a manifest authority, a clear proof, to Fir'awn and his chiefs, but they followed the command of Fir'awn, and opposed the command of Musa; and the command of Fir'awn was not right. He will lead his people (yaqdumu qawmahu), that is, go before them and lead them to the Fire on the Day of Resurrection, and He brought them down to the Fire; and wretched is the place of arrival (al-wird al-mawrud), the entrance into which they were put.

And they were followed in this world by a curse, and on the Day of Resurrection; wretched is the gift (rifd) given (al-marfud), the help that is supplied. That is because curses were heaped upon them: a curse in this world and a curse in the Hereafter.

That is among the tidings of the towns which We relate to you: some still standing and some reaped (destroyed). Ibn Abbas: "Standing" means they can be seen; "reaped" means it has been ruined and its people perished. Muqatil: "Standing" means it has a trace; "reaped" means it has no trace. Mujahid: "Standing" means: "fallen upon its roofs"; "reaped": "uprooted," meaning cut down like the crop when harvested. Qatadah said: "Of them, the standing one has not disappeared at all, and of them is the reaped one which has completely disappeared." al-Qurazi: "Of them standing, with its walls and partitions; and reaped: fallen." Muhammad ibn Ishaq: "Of them standing, meaning [.....] [[unreadable word.]] and similar towns that were not destroyed; and reaped, meaning those that were destroyed."

We did not wrong them by the punishment and destruction, but they wronged themselves by disbelief and disobedience. So their gods that they called upon besides Allah did not avail them anything when the command of your Lord came; and they added nothing to them but ruin (tatbib), that is, loss.

And thus is the seizing of your Lord when He seizes the towns while they are doing wrong. Indeed His seizure is painful and severe. It is similar to His saying: "Indeed the grip of your Lord is severe."

Indeed in that is a lesson and admonition for those who fear the punishment of the Hereafter. That, meaning the Day of Resurrection, is a day on which people will be gathered. Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said to his companions: "You will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection in one plain, hearing the caller [.....] [[unreadable word.]]." And that is a witnessed day, witnessed by the people of the heavens and the people of the earth.

And We do not delay it, meaning We do not delay that day nor establish the Resurrection upon you, except for a determined term, that is, a fixed time that will neither advance nor delay. "On the day it comes" — it is read with the letter ya' affirmed and deleted; both are dialects. The deletion of the ya' has two ways, like the kasrah [replacing] the ya' and the dammah from the waw, as the poet said: [see note]. "No soul speaks except by His permission," like His saying: "The angels descend," meaning: "are sent down."

Labid said:
"And the eye pouring over its young ones
— the sheep (?) — fading in the wide space with its wings."
[That is, "ta'ajjal" (is delayed/hastened).]

So among them are wretched and happy. Ibn Abbas said: "Among them the wretched is the one for whom wretchedness was written; [and the happy is the one for whom happiness was written]."

Abd Allah ibn Dinar narrated from Ibn Umar, from Umar, who said: When this verse was revealed I asked the Prophet (ﷺ), saying: "O Prophet of Allah, then on what do we act: on something already finished, or on something not yet finished?" He (ﷺ) said: "On something already finished, O Umar, and the pens have run with it, but each is made easy for what he was created for."

And it is narrated from him (peace be upon him): "The wretched is one who is wretched in his mother's womb, and the happy is one who is happy in his mother's womb."

As for those who are wretched, they are in the Fire, abiding therein; for them therein is a groaning (zafir) and a sighing (shahiq). Ibn Abbas said: "Zafir is the loud sound, and shahiq is the weak sound." Al-Dahhak and Muqatil: "Zafir is the first braying of the donkey, and shahiq is its end, when it finishes its sound after repeating it in the belly." Abu al-Aliyah: "Zafir is in the throat, and shahiq is in the chest." Abiding therein, remaining and dwelling therein, "as long as the heavens and the earth endure." Here "ma" is called a time-word.

Ibn Abbas said: "As long as the heavens and the earth endure," from their beginning until the time of their passing away. Al-Dahhak said: "As long as the heavens and earths of Paradise and Hell last, and everything above you that shades you is a heaven, and everything on which your foot rests is earth." Al-Husayn said: "He intended: as long as the Hereafter lasts, like the enduring of the heavens and the earth in this world, measuring the duration of their existence." The people of meanings said: "The Arabs [ ... ] [[unreadable speech.]] in the sense of perpetuity and eternity; they say: 'it remains as long as [ ... ] [[unreadable word.]] the camel moaned, the fruit ripened, the tree leafed, the night was dark, a stream flowed, a visitor knocked, the sun rose, the speaker spoke, as long as night and day alternate, as long as the spark and the ember differ, as long as the palm-stalk remains, as long as the white-coated mare's teeth gleam.'" "As long as the heavens and the earth endure": so Allah addressed them with what they knew among themselves.

Then He made an exception, saying: "Except what your Lord wills." The scholars differed concerning these two exceptions, whether they concern the people of wretchedness or the people of happiness. Some said it concerns the people of monotheism whom Allah will bring out of the Fire. Ibn Abbas said: "'Except what your Lord wills' — that He brings the people of monotheism out of it." And he said, concerning His description of the happy: "Except what your Lord wills," that He may make them abide in Paradise. Qatadah said: "Allah knows best regarding this verse; it has been mentioned to us that what I say will touch them: a burning from the Fire for sins they committed, then Allah will bring them out of it." On this view the exception is from a different category, because the wretched in reality are the disbelievers, and the happy in reality are the believers.

Abu Majlaz said: "It is their recompense, except that your Lord wills to pardon them and not enter them into the Fire; and in the description of the happy: 'except what your Lord wills' — their remaining in Paradise." Ibn Mas'ud said: "'Abiding therein as long as the heavens and earth endure': they do not die therein nor come out of it, except what your Lord wills. That is that He commands the Fire to consume them and annihilate them, then He renews their creation." He said: "And there will surely come upon Hell a time when its gates will be closed, with no one in it; and that is after they have remained therein for ages (ahqab)." al-Sha'bi said: "Hell is the swiftest of the two abodes in ageing and the swiftest in ruin." Ibn Zayd said: "In this verse He told us of what He created for the people of Paradise, saying: 'This is an unending gift,' and He did not tell us of what He created for the people of the Fire." Ibn Kaysan said: "'Except what your Lord wills' concerns both groups: their lengthening of life in this world before they go to Paradise or the Fire." It was also said: "'What your Lord wills' concerns the detention of both groups in the barzakh between death and resurrection."

al-Zajjaj: "In this verse there are four opinions: two of them from the linguists, and two from the people of meanings. As for one of the two linguistic opinions, they said: 'illa' here means 'except' in the sense of 'besides,' as one says in speech: 'There was no man with us except Zayd,' and 'I have on you a thousand dirhams except the two thousand that are mine upon you.' So the meaning is: 'as long as the heavens and earth endure, besides what your Lord wills of eternity.' The second opinion: He made an exception from the removal, though He does not intend to remove them from it, as one says: 'I wanted to do such-and-such except if I should wish otherwise,' while you remain upon that act. The meaning is that if He willed to remove them He would have removed them, but He informed them that they are abiding therein." al-Zajjaj said: "These are the two positions of the linguists."

As for the two positions of the people of meanings: they said: "'Abiding therein as long as the heavens and earth endure, except what your Lord wills' — from the measure of their standing at the graves of their graves and for the reckoning," and "except what your Lord wills" — an increase of bliss for the people of bliss, and an increase of punishment for the people of Hell. al-Farra' said: "Its meaning: your Lord has willed the abiding of these in the Fire and these in Paradise," and "illa" in the sense of "waw" (and) is permissible in the language. Allah said: "That mankind may have no argument against you, except those of them who did wrong" — and its meaning is "nor those who did wrong." And Abu Thawran recited to me:

"Whoever shared in the scattering of Falij,
his camels were smitten together and they went forth,
Except like the one who abandoned you,
like a branch in its arrogance, rooted."

Its meaning: "but here [it is] like Nashirah," which is like the name of a tribe. He said: its meaning is "as your Lord has willed," like His saying: "And do not marry those whom your fathers married of women, except what has already passed," meaning "as has already passed."

As for those who are made happy: the people of Kufa read "su'idu" with a dammah on the sin, meaning they were granted happiness; "sa'ida" and "as'ada" have the same meaning. The rest read with a fatha on the sin, analogically with "those who were made wretched," and this was preferred by Abu Ubayd and Abu Hatim. "Then in Paradise they abide therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills." al-Dahhak: "Except what they remained in the Fire until they were admitted to Paradise." Abu Sinan: "Except what your Lord wills of the addition beyond the duration of the heavens and earth, and that is the eternity therein." Allah said: "a gift not cut off," not interrupted.

Wakee' ibn al-Jarrah said: "The Jahmiyyah disbelieved in four verses of the Book of Allah. Allah said in describing the bliss of Paradise: 'neither cut off nor forbidden,' and the Jahmiyyah said: 'it is cut off and then forbidden to them.' Allah said: 'its fruit is perpetual and its shade,' and they said: 'it does not endure.' Allah said: 'what is with you will vanish, and what is with Allah remains,' and they said: 'it does not remain.' Allah said: 'a gift not cut off,' and they said: 'it is cut off and severed.'"

So do not be, O Muhammad, in doubt (mirya) about what these worship; they are misguided. They worship only as their fathers worshipped before; there is an implied ellipsis, i.e., [like the worship of] their fathers before. Indeed We will surely give them their share, their portion of recompense, without diminution.

And to Madyan [We sent] their brother Shu'ayb (the Quran says: "And to Madyan, their brother Shu'ayb"). That is, We sent to the people of Madyan, the son of Ibrahim, their brother Shu'ayb, son of Shurun, son of Ayyub, son of Madyan, son of Ibrahim.

He said: "O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. And do not diminish the measure and the scale, for I see you in prosperity, and I fear for you the punishment of an all-encompassing Day." They used to cheat in measure and weight. Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Affluent and in blessing." al-Hasan: "Wealth and cheap prices." Qatadah: "Property and the adornment of this world." al-Dahhak: "Abundant living and much wealth." Mujahid: "Fertility and abundance." Others said: "[It means] high prices, the loss of blessing and the descent of retribution if they do not repent." "And indeed I fear for you the punishment of an all-encompassing Day," meaning it will encompass you, so none of you will escape.

"And O my people, give full measure and weight; weigh with justice. And do not defraud people of their things," that is, do not diminish people's goods. "And do not commit abuse on the earth, spreading corruption." "What remains with Allah is better for you, if you are believers." Ibn Abbas said: "What Allah has left for you of lawful gain." Giving full measure and weight is better than defrauding and cheating [defrauding and cheating means diminishing the measure and the scale]. Mujahid said: "[It means] obedience." Sufyan [said]: "The provision of Allah." Qatadah: "Your share from your Lord." Ibn Zayd: "Destruction in the punishment." And "al-baqiyyah" [remainder]: "mercy." al-Farra': "Watchfulness of Allah." "And I am not a guardian over you." He said this because Shu'ayb had not been commanded to fight.

They said: "O Shu'ayb, does your prayer command you that we abandon what our fathers worshipped of idols, or that we stop doing what we wish with our wealth?" Ibn Abbas said: "Shu'ayb used to pray much, so they said this." al-A'mash said: "[It means] your recitation." "Or that we should not do with our wealth what we wish," that is, or that we should give up doing with our wealth what we wish. Some read "tafʿalu" and "tashaʾu" with the letter ta, meaning: "your command is that you do with our wealth what you wish," so that it refers to the command and not to the abandoning.

The people of tafsir (exegesis) said: "This was a prohibition for them, and they were punished for it: they cut the dinars and dirhams. Therefore they said: 'And that we do with our wealth what we wish.'" "Indeed you are the forbearing, the upright." Ibn Abbas said: "The foolish, the misguided." al-Qadi said: "The Arabs describe a thing by its opposite, out of euphemism and good omen, as they said of the stung person: 'Safe' (salim), and of the desert: 'mafaza' (a place of escape)."

It was also said that it is said in mockery, like their saying to the Abyssinian: "Father of the white," and to the white man: "Father of the black," and from it is the saying of the guardians of the Fire to Abu Jahl: "Taste it; indeed you are the mighty, the noble." It was said: its meaning is "the forbearing, the upright" according to your claim, and in the opinion of Abu Jahl the same. Ibn Kaysan said: it is meant literally, that is, "Indeed you, O Shu'ayb, are forbearing and upright among us," so it does not befit you to split the unity of your people or oppose their religion, like the saying of the people of Salih to him: "O Salih, you were among us a hoped-for one."

He said: "O my people, do you see? If I am upon a clear proof (bayyinah), from my Lord, and He has given me a good provision from Him," meaning proof, insight, clarification and evidence; "and He has given me good provision from Him," lawful and good, without defrauding or cheating. It was also said: knowledge and understanding. "And I do not wish to oppose you by doing what I forbid you from. I wish only reform as far as I am able. My success is only through Allah; upon Him I rely, and to Him I turn back," that is, I return to Him in whatever calamities befall me. It was also said: to Him I return in the Hereafter.

"And O my people, let not my dissension (shiqaq) cause you [to commit] — let not my opposition and separation induce you — that there befall you the like of what befell the people of Nuh, or the people of Hud, or the people of Salih," of punishment; "and the people of Lut are not far from you." That is because they were recent in time to the destruction of the people of Lut. It was also said: the dwelling of the people of Lut is not far from you. "And O my people, seek forgiveness of your Lord, then turn to Him in repentance. Indeed my Lord is Merciful, Loving (wadud)," loving the believers. It was also said: beloved to the believers and loved by them.

They said: "O Shu'ayb, we do not understand much of what you say, and indeed we see you among us as weak." That was because he was blind. Sufyan said: "He was weak of sight," and it was said of him: "the orator of the prophets." "And were it not for your clan," your tribe, and he had might and protection from his people, "we would have stoned you," we would have killed you. "And you are not mighty against us."

He said: "O my people, is my clan more esteemed by you than Allah, and you have cast Him behind your backs?" It was said: the pronoun refers to Allah; and it was said: to the command of Allah and what Shu'ayb brought, meaning you have thrown it behind your backs and abandoned it. It is said: "I placed my affair behind my back" when one neglects his affair and fails in his duty.

"Indeed my Lord is encompassing of what you do. And O my people, act according to your position (makanah)," that is, your deliberation and station. It is said: "So-and-so acts according to his status (makanah) and standing (makanah)" when he acts with deliberation and settles. And it is said: "makana, yamkunu, makanan, makanah." "Indeed I am acting; you will know" which of us is the one who brings harm upon himself and is more misguided in his action. That is His saying: "Who will receive a punishment that disgraces him, and who is a liar." It was said: ("man") is in the accusative position, meaning "you will know who is the liar." It was also said: "and He will disgrace the one who is a liar." It was also said: its position is nominative, its estimation being: "and who is a liar, so his lie will be known, and he will taste the consequence of his affair." "So wait," and expect the punishment. "Indeed I am with you as a watcher, expecting."

When Our command came, We saved Shu'ayb and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us, and the Cry seized those who did wrong: a cry from the sky seized them and destroyed them. It is said: Jibril cried out at them with one cry, and their souls left their bodies.

So they were found in their homes, prostrate, dead, fallen, slain, as if they had never dwelt there. "Away with them!" Destruction and wrath, "as Madyan was made distant" when Thamud perished.

And We certainly sent Musa with Our signs and a manifest authority, a clear proof, to Fir'awn and his chiefs, but they followed the command of Fir'awn, and opposed the command of Musa; and the command of Fir'awn was not right. He will lead his people (yaqdumu qawmahu), that is, go before them and lead them to the Fire on the Day of Resurrection, and He brought them down to the Fire; and wretched is the place of arrival (al-wird al-mawrud), the entrance into which they were put.

And they were followed in this world by a curse, and on the Day of Resurrection; wretched is the gift (rifd) given (al-marfud), the help that is supplied. That is because curses were heaped upon them: a curse in this world and a curse in the Hereafter.

That is among the tidings of the towns which We relate to you: some still standing and some reaped (destroyed). Ibn Abbas: "Standing" means they can be seen; "reaped" means it has been ruined and its people perished. Muqatil: "Standing" means it has a trace; "reaped" means it has no trace. Mujahid: "Standing" means: "fallen upon its roofs"; "reaped": "uprooted," meaning cut down like the crop when harvested. Qatadah said: "Of them, the standing one has not disappeared at all, and of them is the reaped one which has completely disappeared." al-Qurazi: "Of them standing, with its walls and partitions; and reaped: fallen." Muhammad ibn Ishaq: "Of them standing, meaning [.....] [[unreadable word.]] and similar towns that were not destroyed; and reaped, meaning those that were destroyed."

We did not wrong them by the punishment and destruction, but they wronged themselves by disbelief and disobedience. So their gods that they called upon besides Allah did not avail them anything when the command of your Lord came; and they added nothing to them but ruin (tatbib), that is, loss.

And thus is the seizing of your Lord when He seizes the towns while they are doing wrong. Indeed His seizure is painful and severe. It is similar to His saying: "Indeed the grip of your Lord is severe."

Indeed in that is a lesson and admonition for those who fear the punishment of the Hereafter. That, meaning the Day of Resurrection, is a day on which people will be gathered. Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said to his companions: "You will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection in one plain, hearing the caller [.....] [[unreadable word.]]." And that is a witnessed day, witnessed by the people of the heavens and the people of the earth.

And We do not delay it, meaning We do not delay that day nor establish the Resurrection upon you, except for a determined term, that is, a fixed time that will neither advance nor delay. "On the day it comes" — it is read with the letter ya' affirmed and deleted; both are dialects. The deletion of the ya' has two ways, like the kasrah [replacing] the ya' and the dammah from the waw, as the poet said: [see note]. "No soul speaks except by His permission," like His saying: "The angels descend," meaning: "are sent down."

Labid said:
"And the eye pouring over its young ones
— the sheep (?) — fading in the wide space with its wings."
[That is, "ta'ajjal" (is delayed/hastened).]

So among them are wretched and happy. Ibn Abbas said: "Among them the wretched is the one for whom wretchedness was written; [and the happy is the one for whom happiness was written]."

Abd Allah ibn Dinar narrated from Ibn Umar, from Umar, who said: When this verse was revealed I asked the Prophet (ﷺ), saying: "O Prophet of Allah, then on what do we act: on something already finished, or on something not yet finished?" He (ﷺ) said: "On something already finished, O Umar, and the pens have run with it, but each is made easy for what he was created for."

And it is narrated from him (peace be upon him): "The wretched is one who is wretched in his mother's womb, and the happy is one who is happy in his mother's womb."

As for those who are wretched, they are in the Fire, abiding therein; for them therein is a groaning (zafir) and a sighing (shahiq). Ibn Abbas said: "Zafir is the loud sound, and shahiq is the weak sound." Al-Dahhak and Muqatil: "Zafir is the first braying of the donkey, and shahiq is its end, when it finishes its sound after repeating it in the belly." Abu al-Aliyah: "Zafir is in the throat, and shahiq is in the chest." Abiding therein, remaining and dwelling therein, "as long as the heavens and the earth endure." Here "ma" is called a time-word.

Ibn Abbas said: "As long as the heavens and the earth endure," from their beginning until the time of their passing away. Al-Dahhak said: "As long as the heavens and earths of Paradise and Hell last, and everything above you that shades you is a heaven, and everything on which your foot rests is earth." Al-Husayn said: "He intended: as long as the Hereafter lasts, like the enduring of the heavens and the earth in this world, measuring the duration of their existence." The people of meanings said: "The Arabs [ ... ] [[unreadable speech.]] in the sense of perpetuity and eternity; they say: 'it remains as long as [ ... ] [[unreadable word.]] the camel moaned, the fruit ripened, the tree leafed, the night was dark, a stream flowed, a visitor knocked, the sun rose, the speaker spoke, as long as night and day alternate, as long as the spark and the ember differ, as long as the palm-stalk remains, as long as the white-coated mare's teeth gleam.'" "As long as the heavens and the earth endure": so Allah addressed them with what they knew among themselves.

Then He made an exception, saying: "Except what your Lord wills." The scholars differed concerning these two exceptions, whether they concern the people of wretchedness or the people of happiness. Some said it concerns the people of monotheism whom Allah will bring out of the Fire. Ibn Abbas said: "'Except what your Lord wills' — that He brings the people of monotheism out of it." And he said, concerning His description of the happy: "Except what your Lord wills," that He may make them abide in Paradise. Qatadah said: "Allah knows best regarding this verse; it has been mentioned to us that what I say will touch them: a burning from the Fire for sins they committed, then Allah will bring them out of it." On this view the exception is from a different category, because the wretched in reality are the disbelievers, and the happy in reality are the believers.

Abu Majlaz said: "It is their recompense, except that your Lord wills to pardon them and not enter them into the Fire; and in the description of the happy: 'except what your Lord wills' — their remaining in Paradise." Ibn Mas'ud said: "'Abiding therein as long as the heavens and earth endure': they do not die therein nor come out of it, except what your Lord wills. That is that He commands the Fire to consume them and annihilate them, then He renews their creation." He said: "And there will surely come upon Hell a time when its gates will be closed, with no one in it; and that is after they have remained therein for ages (ahqab)." al-Sha'bi said: "Hell is the swiftest of the two abodes in ageing and the swiftest in ruin." Ibn Zayd said: "In this verse He told us of what He created for the people of Paradise, saying: 'This is an unending gift,' and He did not tell us of what He created for the people of the Fire." Ibn Kaysan said: "'Except what your Lord wills' concerns both groups: their lengthening of life in this world before they go to Paradise or the Fire." It was also said: "'What your Lord wills' concerns the detention of both groups in the barzakh between death and resurrection."

al-Zajjaj: "In this verse there are four opinions: two of them from the linguists, and two from the people of meanings. As for one of the two linguistic opinions, they said: 'illa' here means 'except' in the sense of 'besides,' as one says in speech: 'There was no man with us except Zayd,' and 'I have on you a thousand dirhams except the two thousand that are mine upon you.' So the meaning is: 'as long as the heavens and earth endure, besides what your Lord wills of eternity.' The second opinion: He made an exception from the removal, though He does not intend to remove them from it, as one says: 'I wanted to do such-and-such except if I should wish otherwise,' while you remain upon that act. The meaning is that if He willed to remove them He would have removed them, but He informed them that they are abiding therein." al-Zajjaj said: "These are the two positions of the linguists."

As for the two positions of the people of meanings: they said: "'Abiding therein as long as the heavens and earth endure, except what your Lord wills' — from the measure of their standing at the graves of their graves and for the reckoning," and "except what your Lord wills" — an increase of bliss for the people of bliss, and an increase of punishment for the people of Hell. al-Farra' said: "Its meaning: your Lord has willed the abiding of these in the Fire and these in Paradise," and "illa" in the sense of "waw" (and) is permissible in the language. Allah said: "That mankind may have no argument against you, except those of them who did wrong" — and its meaning is "nor those who did wrong." And Abu Thawran recited to me:

"Whoever shared in the scattering of Falij,
his camels were smitten together and they went forth,
Except like the one who abandoned you,
like a branch in its arrogance, rooted."

Its meaning: "but here [it is] like Nashirah," which is like the name of a tribe. He said: its meaning is "as your Lord has willed," like His saying: "And do not marry those whom your fathers married of women, except what has already passed," meaning "as has already passed."

As for those who are made happy: the people of Kufa read "su'idu" with a dammah on the sin, meaning they were granted happiness; "sa'ida" and "as'ada" have the same meaning. The rest read with a fatha on the sin, analogically with "those who were made wretched," and this was preferred by Abu Ubayd and Abu Hatim. "Then in Paradise they abide therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills." al-Dahhak: "Except what they remained in the Fire until they were admitted to Paradise." Abu Sinan: "Except what your Lord wills of the addition beyond the duration of the heavens and earth, and that is the eternity therein." Allah said: "a gift not cut off," not interrupted.

Wakee' ibn al-Jarrah said: "The Jahmiyyah disbelieved in four verses of the Book of Allah. Allah said in describing the bliss of Paradise: 'neither cut off nor forbidden,' and the Jahmiyyah said: 'it is cut off and then forbidden to them.' Allah said: 'its fruit is perpetual and its shade,' and they said: 'it does not endure.' Allah said: 'what is with you will vanish, and what is with Allah remains,' and they said: 'it does not remain.' Allah said: 'a gift not cut off,' and they said: 'it is cut off and severed.'"

So do not be, O Muhammad, in doubt (mirya) about what these worship; they are misguided. They worship only as their fathers worshipped before; there is an implied ellipsis, i.e., [like the worship of] their fathers before. Indeed We will surely give them their share, their portion of recompense, without diminution.

And to Madyan [We sent] their brother Shu'ayb (the Quran says: "And to Madyan, their brother Shu'ayb"). That is, We sent to the people of Madyan, the son of Ibrahim, their brother Shu'ayb, son of Shurun, son of Ayyub, son of Madyan, son of Ibrahim.

He said: "O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. And do not diminish the measure and the scale, for I see you in prosperity, and I fear for you the punishment of an all-encompassing Day." They used to cheat in measure and weight. Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Affluent and in blessing." al-Hasan: "Wealth and cheap prices." Qatadah: "Property and the adornment of this world." al-Dahhak: "Abundant living and much wealth." Mujahid: "Fertility and abundance." Others said: "[It means] high prices, the loss of blessing and the descent of retribution if they do not repent." "And indeed I fear for you the punishment of an all-encompassing Day," meaning it will encompass you, so none of you will escape.

"And O my people, give full measure and weight; weigh with justice. And do not defraud people of their things," that is, do not diminish people's goods. "And do not commit abuse on the earth, spreading corruption." "What remains with Allah is better for you, if you are believers." Ibn Abbas said: "What Allah has left for you of lawful gain." Giving full measure and weight is better than defrauding and cheating [defrauding and cheating means diminishing the measure and the scale]. Mujahid said: "[It means] obedience." Sufyan [said]: "The provision of Allah." Qatadah: "Your share from your Lord." Ibn Zayd: "Destruction in the punishment." And "al-baqiyyah" [remainder]: "mercy." al-Farra': "Watchfulness of Allah." "And I am not a guardian over you." He said this because Shu'ayb had not been commanded to fight.

They said: "O Shu'ayb, does your prayer command you that we abandon what our fathers worshipped of idols, or that we stop doing what we wish with our wealth?" Ibn Abbas said: "Shu'ayb used to pray much, so they said this." al-A'mash said: "[It means] your recitation." "Or that we should not do with our wealth what we wish," that is, or that we should give up doing with our wealth what we wish. Some read "tafʿalu" and "tashaʾu" with the letter ta, meaning: "your command is that you do with our wealth what you wish," so that it refers to the command and not to the abandoning.

The people of tafsir (exegesis) said: "This was a prohibition for them, and they were punished for it: they cut the dinars and dirhams. Therefore they said: 'And that we do with our wealth what we wish.'" "Indeed you are the forbearing, the upright." Ibn Abbas said: "The foolish, the misguided." al-Qadi said: "The Arabs describe a thing by its opposite, out of euphemism and good omen, as they said of the stung person: 'Safe' (salim), and of the desert: 'mafaza' (a place of escape)."

It was also said that it is said in mockery, like their saying to the Abyssinian: "Father of the white," and to the white man: "Father of the black," and from it is the saying of the guardians of the Fire to Abu Jahl: "Taste it; indeed you are the mighty, the noble." It was said: its meaning is "the forbearing, the upright" according to your claim, and in the opinion of Abu Jahl the same. Ibn Kaysan said: it is meant literally, that is, "Indeed you, O Shu'ayb, are forbearing and upright among us," so it does not befit you to split the unity of your people or oppose their religion, like the saying of the people of Salih to him: "O Salih, you were among us a hoped-for one."

He said: "O my people, do you see? If I am upon a clear proof (bayyinah), from my Lord, and He has given me a good provision from Him," meaning proof, insight, clarification and evidence; "and He has given me good provision from Him," lawful and good, without defrauding or cheating. It was also said: knowledge and understanding. "And I do not wish to oppose you by doing what I forbid you from. I wish only reform as far as I am able. My success is only through Allah; upon Him I rely, and to Him I turn back," that is, I return to Him in whatever calamities befall me. It was also said: to Him I return in the Hereafter.

"And O my people, let not my dissension (shiqaq) cause you [to commit] — let not my opposition and separation induce you — that there befall you the like of what befell the people of Nuh, or the people of Hud, or the people of Salih," of punishment; "and the people of Lut are not far from you." That is because they were recent in time to the destruction of the people of Lut. It was also said: the dwelling of the people of Lut is not far from you. "And O my people, seek forgiveness of your Lord, then turn to Him in repentance. Indeed my Lord is Merciful, Loving (wadud)," loving the believers. It was also said: beloved to the believers and loved by them.

They said: "O Shu'ayb, we do not understand much of what you say, and indeed we see you among us as weak." That was because he was blind. Sufyan said: "He was weak of sight," and it was said of him: "the orator of the prophets." "And were it not for your clan," your tribe, and he had might and protection from his people, "we would have stoned you," we would have killed you. "And you are not mighty against us."

He said: "O my people, is my clan more esteemed by you than Allah, and you have cast Him behind your backs?" It was said: the pronoun refers to Allah; and it was said: to the command of Allah and what Shu'ayb brought, meaning you have thrown it behind your backs and abandoned it. It is said: "I placed my affair behind my back" when one neglects his affair and fails in his duty.

"Indeed my Lord is encompassing of what you do. And O my people, act according to your position (makanah)," that is, your deliberation and station. It is said: "So-and-so acts according to his status (makanah) and standing (makanah)" when he acts with deliberation and settles. And it is said: "makana, yamkunu, makanan, makanah." "Indeed I am acting; you will know" which of us is the one who brings harm upon himself and is more misguided in his action. That is His saying: "Who will receive a punishment that disgraces him, and who is a liar." It was said: ("man") is in the accusative position, meaning "you will know who is the liar." It was also said: "and He will disgrace the one who is a liar." It was also said: its position is nominative, its estimation being: "and who is a liar, so his lie will be known, and he will taste the consequence of his affair." "So wait," and expect the punishment. "Indeed I am with you as a watcher, expecting."

When Our command came, We saved Shu'ayb and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us, and the Cry seized those who did wrong: a cry from the sky seized them and destroyed them. It is said: Jibril cried out at them with one cry, and their souls left their bodies.

So they were found in their homes, prostrate, dead, fallen, slain, as if they had never dwelt there. "Away with them!" Destruction and wrath, "as Madyan was made distant" when Thamud perished.

And We certainly sent Musa with Our signs and a manifest authority, a clear proof, to Fir'awn and his chiefs, but they followed the command of Fir'awn, and opposed the command of Musa; and the command of Fir'awn was not right. He will lead his people (yaqdumu qawmahu), that is, go before them and lead them to the Fire on the Day of Resurrection, and He brought them down to the Fire; and wretched is the place of arrival (al-wird al-mawrud), the entrance into which they were put.

And they were followed in this world by a curse, and on the Day of Resurrection; wretched is the gift (rifd) given (al-marfud), the help that is supplied. That is because curses were heaped upon them: a curse in this world and a curse in the Hereafter.

That is among the tidings of the towns which We relate to you: some still standing and some reaped (destroyed). Ibn Abbas: "Standing" means they can be seen; "reaped" means it has been ruined and its people perished. Muqatil: "Standing" means it has a trace; "reaped" means it has no trace. Mujahid: "Standing" means: "fallen upon its roofs"; "reaped": "uprooted," meaning cut down like the crop when harvested. Qatadah said: "Of them, the standing one has not disappeared at all, and of them is the reaped one which has completely disappeared." al-Qurazi: "Of them standing, with its walls and partitions; and reaped: fallen." Muhammad ibn Ishaq: "Of them standing, meaning [.....] [[unreadable word.]] and similar towns that were not destroyed; and reaped, meaning those that were destroyed."

We did not wrong them by the punishment and destruction, but they wronged themselves by disbelief and disobedience. So their gods that they called upon besides Allah did not avail them anything when the command of your Lord came; and they added nothing to them but ruin (tatbib), that is, loss.

And thus is the seizing of your Lord when He seizes the towns while they are doing wrong. Indeed His seizure is painful and severe. It is similar to His saying: "Indeed the grip of your Lord is severe."

Indeed in that is a lesson and admonition for those who fear the punishment of the Hereafter. That, meaning the Day of Resurrection, is a day on which people will be gathered. Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said to his companions: "You will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection in one plain, hearing the caller [.....] [[unreadable word.]]." And that is a witnessed day, witnessed by the people of the heavens and the people of the earth.

And We do not delay it, meaning We do not delay that day nor establish the Resurrection upon you, except for a determined term, that is, a fixed time that will neither advance nor delay. "On the day it comes" — it is read with the letter ya' affirmed and deleted; both are dialects. The deletion of the ya' has two ways, like the kasrah [replacing] the ya' and the dammah from the waw, as the poet said: [see note]. "No soul speaks except by His permission," like His saying: "The angels descend," meaning: "are sent down."

Labid said:
"And the eye pouring over its young ones
— the sheep (?) — fading in the wide space with its wings."
[That is, "ta'ajjal" (is delayed/hastened).]

So among them are wretched and happy. Ibn Abbas said: "Among them the wretched is the one for whom wretchedness was written; [and the happy is the one for whom happiness was written]."

Abd Allah ibn Dinar narrated from Ibn Umar, from Umar, who said: When this verse was revealed I asked the Prophet (ﷺ), saying: "O Prophet of Allah, then on what do we act: on something already finished, or on something not yet finished?" He (ﷺ) said: "On something already finished, O Umar, and the pens have run with it, but each is made easy for what he was created for."

And it is narrated from him (peace be upon him): "The wretched is one who is wretched in his mother's womb, and the happy is one who is happy in his mother's womb."

As for those who are wretched, they are in the Fire, abiding therein; for them therein is a groaning (zafir) and a sighing (shahiq). Ibn Abbas said: "Zafir is the loud sound, and shahiq is the weak sound." Al-Dahhak and Muqatil: "Zafir is the first braying of the donkey, and shahiq is its end, when it finishes its sound after repeating it in the belly." Abu al-Aliyah: "Zafir is in the throat, and shahiq is in the chest." Abiding therein, remaining and dwelling therein, "as long as the heavens and the earth endure." Here "ma" is called a time-word.

Ibn Abbas said: "As long as the heavens and the earth endure," from their beginning until the time of their passing away. Al-Dahhak said: "As long as the heavens and earths of Paradise and Hell last, and everything above you that shades you is a heaven, and everything on which your foot rests is earth." Al-Husayn said: "He intended: as long as the Hereafter lasts, like the enduring of the heavens and the earth in this world, measuring the duration of their existence." The people of meanings said: "The Arabs [ ... ] [[unreadable speech.]] in the sense of perpetuity and eternity; they say: 'it remains as long as [ ... ] [[unreadable word.]] the camel moaned, the fruit ripened, the tree leafed, the night was dark, a stream flowed, a visitor knocked, the sun rose, the speaker spoke, as long as night and day alternate, as long as the spark and the ember differ, as long as the palm-stalk remains, as long as the white-coated mare's teeth gleam.'" "As long as the heavens and the earth endure": so Allah addressed them with what they knew among themselves.

Then He made an exception, saying: "Except what your Lord wills." The scholars differed concerning these two exceptions, whether they concern the people of wretchedness or the people of happiness. Some said it concerns the people of monotheism whom Allah will bring out of the Fire. Ibn Abbas said: "'Except what your Lord wills' — that He brings the people of monotheism out of it." And he said, concerning His description of the happy: "Except what your Lord wills," that He may make them abide in Paradise. Qatadah said: "Allah knows best regarding this verse; it has been mentioned to us that what I say will touch them: a burning from the Fire for sins they committed, then Allah will bring them out of it." On this view the exception is from a different category, because the wretched in reality are the disbelievers, and the happy in reality are the believers.

Abu Majlaz said: "It is their recompense, except that your Lord wills to pardon them and not enter them into the Fire; and in the description of the happy: 'except what your Lord wills' — their remaining in Paradise." Ibn Mas'ud said: "'Abiding therein as long as the heavens and earth endure': they do not die therein nor come out of it, except what your Lord wills. That is that He commands the Fire to consume them and annihilate them, then He renews their creation." He said: "And there will surely come upon Hell a time when its gates will be closed, with no one in it; and that is after they have remained therein for ages (ahqab)." al-Sha'bi said: "Hell is the swiftest of the two abodes in ageing and the swiftest in ruin." Ibn Zayd said: "In this verse He told us of what He created for the people of Paradise, saying: 'This is an unending gift,' and He did not tell us of what He created for the people of the Fire." Ibn Kaysan said: "'Except what your Lord wills' concerns both groups: their lengthening of life in this world before they go to Paradise or the Fire." It was also said: "'What your Lord wills' concerns the detention of both groups in the barzakh between death and resurrection."

al-Zajjaj: "In this verse there are four opinions: two of them from the linguists, and two from the people of meanings. As for one of the two linguistic opinions, they said: 'illa' here means 'except' in the sense of 'besides,' as one says in speech: 'There was no man with us except Zayd,' and 'I have on you a thousand dirhams except the two thousand that are mine upon you.' So the meaning is: 'as long as the heavens and earth endure, besides what your Lord wills of eternity.' The second opinion: He made an exception from the removal, though He does not intend to remove them from it, as one says: 'I wanted to do such-and-such except if I should wish otherwise,' while you remain upon that act. The meaning is that if He willed to remove them He would have removed them, but He informed them that they are abiding therein." al-Zajjaj said: "These are the two positions of the linguists."

As for the two positions of the people of meanings: they said: "'Abiding therein as long as the heavens and earth endure, except what your Lord wills' — from the measure of their standing at the graves of their graves and for the reckoning," and "except what your Lord wills" — an increase of bliss for the people of bliss, and an increase of punishment for the people of Hell. al-Farra' said: "Its meaning: your Lord has willed the abiding of these in the Fire and these in Paradise," and "illa" in the sense of "waw" (and) is permissible in the language. Allah said: "That mankind may have no argument against you, except those of them who did wrong" — and its meaning is "nor those who did wrong." And Abu Thawran recited to me:

"Whoever shared in the scattering of Falij,
his camels were smitten together and they went forth,
Except like the one who abandoned you,
like a branch in its arrogance, rooted."

Its meaning: "but here [it is] like Nashirah," which is like the name of a tribe. He said: its meaning is "as your Lord has willed," like His saying: "And do not marry those whom your fathers married of women, except what has already passed," meaning "as has already passed."

As for those who are made happy: the people of Kufa read "su'idu" with a dammah on the sin, meaning they were granted happiness; "sa'ida" and "as'ada" have the same meaning. — the sheep (?) — fading in the wide space with its wings."
[That is, "ta'ajjal" (is delayed/hastened).]

So among them are wretched and happy. Ibn Abbas said: "Among them the wretched is the one for whom wretchedness was written; [and the happy is the one for whom happiness was written]."

Abd Allah ibn Dinar narrated from Ibn Umar, from Umar, who said: When this verse was revealed I asked the Prophet (ﷺ), saying: "O Prophet of Allah, then on what do we act: on something already finished, or on something not yet finished?" He (ﷺ) said: "On something already finished, O Umar, and the pens have run with it, but each is made easy for what he was created for."

And it is narrated from him (peace be upon him): "The wretched is one who is wretched in his mother's womb, and the happy is one who is happy in his mother's womb."

As for those who are wretched, they are in the Fire, abiding therein; for them therein is a groaning (zafir) and a sighing (shahiq). Ibn Abbas said: "Zafir is the loud sound, and shahiq is the weak sound." Al-Dahhak and Muqatil: "Zafir is the first braying of the donkey, and shahiq is its end, when it finishes its sound after repeating it in the belly." Abu al-Aliyah: "Zafir is in the throat, and shahiq is in the chest." Abiding therein, remaining and dwelling therein, "as long as the heavens and the earth endure." Here "ma" is called a time-word.

Ibn Abbas said: "As long as the heavens and the earth endure," from their beginning until the time of their passing away. Al-Dahhak said: "As long as the heavens and earths of Paradise and Hell last, and everything above you that shades you is a heaven, and everything on which your foot rests is earth." Al-Husayn said: "He intended: as long as the Hereafter lasts, like the enduring of the heavens and the earth in this world, measuring the duration of their existence." The people of meanings said: "The Arabs [ ... ] [[unreadable speech.]] in the sense of perpetuity and eternity; they say: 'it remains as long as [ ... ] [[unreadable word.]] the camel moaned, the fruit ripened, the tree leafed, the night was dark, a stream flowed, a visitor knocked, the sun rose, the speaker spoke, as long as night and day alternate, as long as the spark and the ember differ, as long as the palm-stalk remains, as long as the white-coated mare's teeth gleam.'" "As long as the heavens and the earth endure": so Allah addressed them with what they knew among themselves.

Then He made an exception, saying: "Except what your Lord wills." The scholars differed concerning these two exceptions, whether they concern the people of wretchedness or the people of happiness. Some said it concerns the people of monotheism whom Allah will bring out of the Fire. Ibn Abbas said: "'Except what your Lord wills' — that He brings the people of monotheism out of it." And he said, concerning His description of the happy: "Except what your Lord wills," that He may make them abide in Paradise. Qatadah said: "Allah knows best regarding this verse; it has been mentioned to us that what I say will touch them: a burning from the Fire for sins they committed, then Allah will bring them out of it." On this view the exception is from a different category, because the wretched in reality are the disbelievers, and the happy in reality are the believers.

Abu Majlaz said: "It is their recompense, except that your Lord wills to pardon them and not enter them into the Fire; and in the description of the happy: 'except what your Lord wills' — their remaining in Paradise." Ibn Mas'ud said: "'Abiding therein as long as the heavens and earth endure': they do not die therein nor come out of it, except what your Lord wills. That is that He commands the Fire to consume them and annihilate them, then He renews their creation." He said: "And there will surely come upon Hell a time when its gates will be closed, with no one in it; and that is after they have remained therein for ages (ahqab)." al-Sha'bi said: "Hell is the swiftest of the two abodes in ageing and the swiftest in ruin." Ibn Zayd said: "In this verse He told us of what He created for the people of Paradise, saying: 'This is an unending gift,' and He did not tell us of what He created for the people of the Fire." Ibn Kaysan said: "'Except what your Lord wills' concerns both groups: their lengthening of life in this world before they go to Paradise or the Fire." It was also said: "'What your Lord wills' concerns the detention of both groups in the barzakh between death and resurrection."

al-Zajjaj: "In this verse there are four opinions: two of them from the linguists, and two from the people of meanings. As for one of the two linguistic opinions, they said: 'illa' here means 'except' in the sense of 'besides,' as one says in speech: 'There was no man with us except Zayd,' and 'I have on you a thousand dirhams except the two thousand that are mine upon you.' So the meaning is: 'as long as the heavens and earth endure, besides what your Lord wills of eternity.' The second opinion: He made an exception from the removal, though He does not intend to remove them from it, as one says: 'I wanted to do such-and-such except if I should wish otherwise,' while you remain upon that act. The meaning is that if He willed to remove them He would have removed them, but He informed them that they are abiding therein." al-Zajjaj said: "These are the two positions of the linguists."

As for the two positions of the people of meanings: they said: "'Abiding therein as long as the heavens and earth endure, except what your Lord wills' — from the measure of their standing at the graves of their graves and for the reckoning," and "except what your Lord wills" — an increase of bliss for the people of bliss, and an increase of punishment for the people of Hell. al-Farra' said: "Its meaning: your Lord has willed the abiding of these in the Fire and these in Paradise," and "illa" in the sense of "waw" (and) is permissible in the language. Allah said: "That mankind may have no argument against you, except those of them who did wrong" — and its meaning is "nor those who did wrong." And Abu Thawran recited to me:

"Whoever shared in the scattering of Falij,
his camels were smitten together and they went forth,
Except like the one who abandoned you,
like a branch in its arrogance, rooted."

Its meaning: "but here [it is] like Nashirah," which is like the name of a tribe. He said: its meaning is "as your Lord has willed," like His saying: "And do not marry those whom your fathers married of women, except what has already passed," meaning "as has already passed."

As for those who are made happy: the people of Kufa read "su'idu" with a dammah on the sin, meaning they were granted happiness; "sa'ida" and "as'ada" have the same meaning. The rest read with a fatha on the sin, analogically with "those who were made wretched," and this was preferred by Abu Ubayd and Abu Hatim. "Then in Paradise they abide therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills." al-Dahhak: "Except what they remained in the Fire until they were admitted to Paradise." Abu Sinan: "Except what your Lord wills of the addition beyond the duration of the heavens and earth, and that is the eternity therein." Allah said: "a gift not cut off," not interrupted.

Wakee' ibn al-Jarrah said: "The Jahmiyyah disbelieved in four verses of the Book of Allah. Allah said in describing the bliss of Paradise: 'neither cut off nor forbidden,' and the Jahmiyyah said: 'it is cut off and then forbidden to them.' Allah said: 'its fruit is perpetual and its shade,' and they said: 'it does not endure.' Allah said: 'what is with you will vanish, and what is with Allah remains,' and they said: 'it does not remain.' Allah said: 'a gift not cut off,' and they said: 'it is cut off and severed.'"

So do not be, O Muhammad, in doubt (mirya) about what these worship; they are misguided. They worship only as their fathers worshipped before; there is an implied ellipsis, i.e., [like the worship of] their fathers before. Indeed We will surely give them their share, their portion of recompense, without diminution.

And to Madyan [We sent] their brother Shu'ayb (the Quran says: "And to Madyan, their brother Shu'ayb"). That is, We sent to the people of Madyan, the son of Ibrahim, their brother Shu'ayb, son of Shurun, son of Ayyub, son of Madyan, son of Ibrahim.

He said: "O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. And do not diminish the measure and the scale, for I see you in prosperity, and I fear for you the punishment of an all-encompassing Day." They used to cheat in measure and weight. Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Affluent and in blessing." al-Hasan: "Wealth and cheap prices." Qatadah: "Property and the adornment of this world." al-Dahhak: "Abundant living and much wealth." Mujahid: "Fertility and abundance." Others said: "[It means] high prices, the loss of blessing and the descent of retribution if they do not repent." "And indeed I fear for you the punishment of an all-encompassing Day," meaning it will encompass you, so none of you will escape.

"And O my people, give full measure and weight; weigh with justice. And do not defraud people of their things," that is, do not diminish people's goods. "And do not commit abuse on the earth, spreading corruption." "What remains with Allah is better for you, if you are believers." Ibn Abbas said: "What Allah has left for you of lawful gain." Giving full measure and weight is better than defrauding and cheating [defrauding and cheating means diminishing the measure and the scale]. Mujahid said: "[It means] obedience." Sufyan [said]: "The provision of Allah." Qatadah: "Your share from your Lord." Ibn Zayd: "Destruction in the punishment." And "al-baqiyyah" [remainder]: "mercy." al-Farra': "Watchfulness of Allah." "And I am not a guardian over you." He said this because Shu'ayb had not been commanded to fight.

They said: "O Shu'ayb, does your prayer command you that we abandon what our fathers worshipped of idols, or that we stop doing what we wish with our wealth?" Ibn Abbas said: "Shu'ayb used to pray much, so they said this." al-A'mash said: "[It means] your recitation." "Or that we should not do with our wealth what we wish," that is, or that we should give up doing with our wealth what we wish. Some read "tafʿalu" and "tashaʾu" with the letter ta, meaning: "your command is that you do with our wealth what you wish," so that it refers to the command and not to the abandoning.

The people of tafsir (exegesis) said: "This was a prohibition for them, and they were punished for it: they cut the dinars and dirhams. Therefore they said: 'And that we do with our wealth what we wish.'" "Indeed you are the forbearing, the upright." Ibn Abbas said: "The foolish, the misguided." al-Qadi said: "The Arabs describe a thing by its opposite, out of euphemism and good omen, as they said of the stung person: 'Safe' (salim), and of the desert: 'mafaza' (a place of escape)."

It was also said that it is said in mockery, like their saying to the Abyssinian: "Father of the white," and to the white man: "Father of the black," and from it is the saying of the guardians of the Fire to Abu Jahl: "Taste it; indeed you are the mighty, the noble." It was said: its meaning is "the forbearing, the upright" according to your claim, and in the opinion of Abu Jahl the same. Ibn Kaysan said: it is meant literally, that is, "Indeed you, O Shu'ayb, are forbearing and upright among us," so it does not befit you to split the unity of your people or oppose their religion, like the saying of the people of Salih to him: "O Salih, you were among us a hoped-for one."

He said: "O my people, do you see? If I am upon a clear proof (bayyinah), from my Lord, and He has given me a good provision from Him," meaning proof, insight, clarification and evidence; "and He has given me good provision from Him," lawful and good, without defrauding or cheating. It was also said: knowledge and understanding. "And I do not wish to oppose you by doing what I forbid you from. I wish only reform as far as I am able. My success is only through Allah; upon Him I rely, and to Him I turn back," that is, I return to Him in whatever calamities befall me. It was also said: to Him I return in the Hereafter.

"And O my people, let not my dissension (shiqaq) cause you [to commit] — let not my opposition and separation induce you — that there befall you the like of what befell the people of Nuh, or the people of Hud, or the people of Salih," of punishment; "and the people of Lut are not far from you." That is because they were recent in time to the destruction of the people of Lut. It was also said: the dwelling of the people of Lut is not far from you. "And O my people, seek forgiveness of your Lord, then turn to Him in repentance. Indeed my Lord is Merciful, Loving (wadud)," loving the believers. It was also said: beloved to the believers and loved by them.

They said: "O Shu'ayb, we do not understand much of what you say, and indeed we see you among us as weak." That was because he was blind. Sufyan said: "He was weak of sight," and it was said of him: "the orator of the prophets." "And were it not for your clan," your tribe, and he had might and protection from his people, "we would have stoned you," we would have killed you. "And you are not mighty against us."

He said: "O my people, is my clan more esteemed by you than Allah, and you have cast Him behind your backs?" It was said: the pronoun refers to Allah; and it was said: to the command of Allah and what Shu'ayb brought, meaning you have thrown it behind your backs and abandoned it. It is said: "I placed my affair behind my back" when one neglects his affair and fails in his duty.

"Indeed my Lord is encompassing of what you do. And O my people, act according to your position (makanah)," that is, your deliberation and station. It is said: "So-and-so acts according to his status (makanah) and standing (makanah)" when he acts with deliberation and settles. And it is said: "makana, yamkunu, makanan, makanah." "Indeed I am acting; you will know" which of us is the one who brings harm upon himself and is more misguided in his action. That is His saying: "Who will receive a punishment that disgraces him, and who is a liar." It was said: ("man") is in the accusative position, meaning "you will know who is the liar." It was also said: "and He will disgrace the one who is a liar." It was also said: its position is nominative, its estimation being: "and who is a liar, so his lie will be known, and he will taste the consequence of his affair." "So wait," and expect the punishment. "Indeed I am with you as a watcher, expecting."

When Our command came, We saved Shu'ayb and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us, and the Cry seized those who did wrong: a cry from the sky seized them and destroyed them. It is said: Jibril cried out at them with one cry, and their souls left their bodies.

So they were found in their homes, prostrate, dead, fallen, slain, as if they had never dwelt there. "Away with them!" Destruction and wrath, "as Madyan was made distant" when Thamud perished.

And We certainly sent Musa with Our signs and a manifest authority, a clear proof, to Fir'awn and his chiefs, but they followed the command of Fir'awn, and opposed the command of Musa; and the command of Fir'awn was not right. He will lead his people (yaqdumu qawmahu), that is, go before them and lead them to the Fire on the Day of Resurrection, and He brought them down to the Fire; and wretched is the place of arrival (al-wird al-mawrud), the entrance into which they were put.

And they were followed in this world by a curse, and on the Day of Resurrection; wretched is the gift (rifd) given (al-marfud), the help that is supplied. That is because curses were heaped upon them: a curse in this world and a curse in the Hereafter.

That is among the tidings of the towns which We relate to you: some still standing and some reaped (destroyed). Ibn Abbas: "Standing" means they can be seen; "reaped" means it has been ruined and its people perished. Muqatil: "Standing" means it has a trace; "reaped" means it has no trace. Mujahid: "Standing" means: "fallen upon its roofs"; "reaped": "uprooted," meaning cut down like the crop when harvested. Qatadah said: "Of them, the standing one has not disappeared at all, and of them is the reaped one which has completely disappeared." al-Qurazi: "Of them standing, with its walls and partitions; and reaped: fallen." Muhammad ibn Ishaq: "Of them standing, meaning [.....] [[unreadable word.]] and similar towns that were not destroyed; and reaped, meaning those that were destroyed."

We did not wrong them by the punishment and destruction, but they wronged themselves by disbelief and disobedience. So their gods that they called upon besides Allah did not avail them anything when the command of your Lord came; and they added nothing to them but ruin (tatbib), that is, loss.

And thus is the seizing of your Lord when He seizes the towns while they are doing wrong. Indeed His seizure is painful and severe. It is similar to His saying: "Indeed the grip of your Lord is severe."

Indeed in that is a lesson and admonition for those who fear the punishment of the Hereafter. That, meaning the Day of Resurrection, is a day on which people will be gathered. Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said to his companions: "You will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection in one plain, hearing the caller [.....] [[unreadable word.]]." And that is a witnessed day, witnessed by the people of the heavens and the people of the earth.

And We do not delay it, meaning We do not delay that day nor establish the Resurrection upon you, except for a determined term, that is, a fixed time that will neither advance nor delay. "On the day it comes" — it is read with the letter ya' affirmed and deleted; both are dialects. The deletion of the ya' has two ways, like the kasrah [replacing] the ya' and the dammah from the waw, as the poet said: [see note]. "No soul speaks except by His permission," like His saying: "The angels descend," meaning: "are sent down."

Labid said:
"And the eye pouring over its young ones
— the sheep (?) — fading in the wide space with its wings."
[That is, "ta'ajjal" (is delayed/hastened).]

So among them are wretched and happy. Ibn Abbas said: "Among them the wretched is the one for whom wretchedness was written; [and the happy is the one for whom happiness was written]."

Abd Allah ibn Dinar narrated from Ibn Umar, from Umar, who said: When this verse was revealed I asked the Prophet (ﷺ), saying: "O Prophet of Allah, then on what do we act: on something already finished, or on something not yet finished?" He (ﷺ) said: "On something already finished, O Umar, and the pens have run with it, but each is made easy for what he was created for."

And it is narrated from him (peace be upon him): "The wretched is one who is wretched in his mother's womb, and the happy is one who is happy in his mother's womb."

As for those who are wretched, they are in the Fire, abiding therein; for them therein is a groaning (zafir) and a sighing (shahiq). Ibn Abbas said: "Zafir is the loud sound, and shahiq is the weak sound." Al-Dahhak and Muqatil: "Zafir is the first braying of the donkey, and shahiq is its end, when it finishes its sound after repeating it in the belly." Al-Dahhak said: "As long as the heavens and earths of Paradise and Hell last, and everything above you that shades you is a heaven, and everything on which your foot rests is earth." Then He made an exception, saying: "Except what your Lord wills." The scholars differed concerning these two exceptions, whether they concern the people of wretchedness or the people of happiness. Some said it concerns the people of monotheism whom Allah will bring out of the Fire. Ibn Abbas said: "'Except what your Lord wills' — that He brings the people of monotheism out of it." And he said, concerning His description of the happy: "Except what your Lord wills," that He may make them abide in Paradise. Qatadah said: "Allah knows best regarding this verse; it has been mentioned to us that what I say will touch them: a burning from the Fire for sins they committed, then Allah will bring them out of it." Abu Majlaz said: "It is their recompense, except that your Lord wills to pardon them and not enter them into the Fire; and in the description of the happy: 'except what your Lord wills' — their remaining in Paradise." Ibn Mas'ud said: "'Abiding therein as long as the heavens and earth endure': they do not die therein nor come out of it, except what your Lord wills. That is that He commands the Fire to consume them and annihilate them, then He renews their creation." It was also said: "'What your Lord wills' concerns the detention of both groups in the barzakh between death and resurrection."

al-Zajjaj: "In this verse there are four opinions: two of them from the linguists, and two from the people of meanings. As for one of the two linguistic opinions, they said: 'illa' here means 'except' in the sense of 'besides,' as one says in speech: 'There was no man with us except Zayd,' and 'I have on you a thousand dirhams except the two thousand that are mine upon you.' The meaning is that if He willed to remove them He would have removed them, but He informed them that they are abiding therein." al-Zajjaj said: "These are the two positions of the linguists."

As for the two positions of the people of meanings: they said: "'Abiding therein as long as the heavens and earth endure, except what your Lord wills' — from the measure of their standing at the graves of their graves and for the reckoning," and "except what your Lord wills" — an increase of bliss for the people of bliss, and an increase of punishment for the people of Hell. al-Farra' said: "Its meaning: your Lord has willed the abiding of these in the Fire and these in Paradise," and "illa" in the sense of "waw" (and) is permissible in the language. "Whoever shared in the scattering of Falij,
his camels were smitten together and they went forth,
Except like the one who abandoned you,
like a branch in its arrogance, rooted."

Indeed We will surely give them their share, their portion of recompense, without diminution.

And to Madyan [We sent] their brother Shu'ayb (the Quran says: "And to Madyan, their brother Shu'ayb"). That is, We sent to the people of Madyan, the son of Ibrahim, their brother Shu'ayb, son of Shurun, son of Ayyub, son of Madyan, son of Ibrahim.
